conversation.content:
Good morning! I’m so glad you were able to come in today. My name is Maya Bennett—I’m a licensed perinatal mental-health clinician here at the women’s clinic. I specialize in helping new mothers sort through the emotional ups-and-downs that can show up after a baby arrives.

Today I’ll be using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—often called the EPDS—to get a quick picture of how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days. It isn’t a test of your parenting; it simply helps us see whether you might benefit from extra emotional support right now. Everything you share stays between you, me, and the clinical team unless you tell me you’re in immediate danger. We’ll go through 10 short questions; most moms finish in under five minutes. There are no right or wrong answers—just whatever is true for you.

Ready to begin? 

In the past week, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly, it feels pretty hard lately. I still laugh once in a while—like if I see something silly on my phone—but it takes effort and it doesn’t feel as natural as it used to. Maybe a couple of times this week, tops.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not very often. I laughed a little one or two times, but mostly it feels forced—like I’m pretending to enjoy things rather than really feeling it.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not much, really. I used to get excited about little plans—like meeting a friend for coffee or even just a walk—but lately it feels like I’m just going through the motions. I can still look forward to a couple of things, but the spark isn’t there the way it was before I had the baby.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby’s fussy or won’t nap, my head jumps straight to “I’m doing something wrong” or “I’m a bad mom.” I know, rationally, babies cry, but I still catch myself thinking it’s my fault more often than not—pretty much several times this week.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yes, definitely. Most days I’ll suddenly feel this knot in my stomach about the baby—like, is he breathing okay, am I holding him right, what if I miss some sign that something’s wrong? There’s no real reason, but the thoughts just keep looping and it’s hard to shut them off. It happens almost daily.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes—like last night I woke up suddenly and my heart was racing because I thought I heard him make a weird sound. It turned out to be nothing, but for a few minutes I felt frozen, almost like I couldn’t breathe. It doesn’t happen every day, but when it does it feels really intense.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes. Most days everything feels like too much—feeding, changing, trying to sleep, the dishes piling up. I keep thinking, “I can’t do all this,” even though I’m still managing. It’s like I’m constantly a step behind and about to drop the ball.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah, that’s been happening. I’ll lie down exhausted, but my mind just keeps spinning with worries about the baby and all the ways I’m probably messing up. It takes me forever to fall asleep, and once I do I still wake up a couple of times with anxious thoughts. I probably get four broken hours a night if I’m lucky.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day this week. It’s not crying-all-day sad, but there’s this heavy, gray feeling that sits on me. I wake up discouraged and it lingers even when I’m doing “normal” things. Sometimes it lifts for a little while, but it always comes back.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

A couple of times this week—usually when everything piles up and I feel like I’m failing. Yesterday the baby wouldn’t settle, the house was a mess, and I just sat on the couch with tears running down. It’s not constant, but those moments hit hard.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

Yeah… it’s popped into my head once or twice, like a quick “what if I just weren’t here” kind of thought. I haven’t made any plans or anything—I’d never leave my baby—but the idea flashes through when I’m really overwhelmed.

You've shared how the past week has felt heavy and overwhelming. The joy you once found in small moments now feels distant, replaced by constant worry about your baby, difficulty sleeping, and a pervasive sense that you're somehow failing as a mom. Even simple tasks feel like too much, and brief flashes of self-harm thoughts have surfaced when the pressure peaks. Your honesty highlights the emotional weight many new mothers carry, and it's clear you're doing your best despite feeling depleted.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 24, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only rare, forced laughter, aligning with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>She reports clear reduction in enjoyment and excitement, matching "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame "a lot," "several times this week," matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-daily intrusive worries about the baby with physical anxiety symptoms and looping thoughts, matching 'Yes, very often</sym>, <sym>Patient describes discrete episodes of sudden nighttime panic with racing heart, breathlessness, and freeze response, consistent with "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most days" and unable to manage routine tasks, aligning with "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty initiating and maintaining sleep due to persistent anxious thoughts, matching "Yes, most of the time".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive, daily low mood that persists despite occasional brief lifts, aligning with "Yes, most of the time".</sym>, <sym>Patient reports fleeting self-harm thoughts "once or twice" when overwhelmed, matching "Sometimes" option</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS score of 24 far exceeds the ≥14 threshold indicating probable major depression with peripartum onset. She endorses <sym>depressed mood most days</sym>, markedly diminished interest (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), <sym>self-blame</sym> nearly daily, <sym>anxiety</sym> and <sym>panic attacks</sym>, <sym>fatigue</sym> coupled with <sym>sleep disruption</sym>, and passive suicidal ideation (Q10 score 2). These symptoms align with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> and mandate urgent evaluation for safety and treatment planning. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange same-day urgent appointment with <med>primary care physician</med> or <med>perinatal psychiatrist</med>
2. Implement continuous supervision until safety plan in place; involve trusted adult at home
3. Provide 24-hour crisis line numbers and local emergency contacts
4. Offer immediate referral to <med>postpartum support group</med> and <med>perinatal therapy services</med>
5. Discuss temporary medication options if medically cleared; emphasize breastfeeding-compatible choices
6. Schedule follow-up EPDS and safety reassessment within one week
7. Encourage brief daily walks and 15-minute rest periods to reduce <sym>hyperarousal</sym>
8. Involve partner or family in nighttime infant care to improve <sym>sleep continuity</sym>
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – Brief Summary

Symptoms & concerns endorsed  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, daily crying spells  
- Marked guilt/self-blame re parenting competence  
- prominent, intrusive, “looping” worries; near-daily anxiety and episodic panic (nocturnal startle, racing heart)  
- Subjective overwhelm, sense of falling behind, fatigue  
- Initial insomnia and middle-night wakening linked to anxious rumination (≈4 broken hrs/night)  
- Passive self-harm ideation (fleeting “what if I weren’t here”); no plan or intent stated

Patterns  
Symptoms present most days × ≥1 week; functional impact on sleep, self-care, and infant-care confidence.

Screening significance  
High endorsement consistent with probable major depressive episode with anxious features in postpartum period; passive suicidal thoughts indicate elevated safety risk.

Risk flags documented for immediate clinical attention and formal assessment.
